QUESTION PRESENTED
Whether the original public meaning of the
Article III “judicial Power” includes the authority to
adjudicate claims and provide remedies for persons
injured by federal officers acting contrary to
constitutional restrictions on their powers and
authority.

INTRODUCTION, SUMMARY, AND
INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE1
Petitioner asks this Court to  overrule Bivens v.
Six Unknown Named Agents of Federal Bureau of
Narcotics, 403 U.S. 388 (1971), because he argues that
holding federal officers personally liable for damages
is inherently a legislative creation, unavailable unless
Congress first authorizes it . But the text and history
of the Constitution show otherwise. The judicial Power
had long been understood to include the authority to
adjudicate claims and provide remedies  w hen a
government officer invaded a private right, such as by
entering a home, seizing goods, or detaining a vessel.
The injured party sued in an ordinary common -law
action, usually trespass. The officer pleaded his
governmental authority as a justification. The court
then exercised judicial power by deciding whether the
law authorized the officer’s conduct. If not, the officer
answered in damages.  Personal officer liability was
not something Congress first had to create by statute.
It was ordinary judicial business : recognizing an
existing right, deciding whether an officer violated it
and whether any defenses applied, and providing an
appropriate remedy.
In Article III’s vesting  the “judicial Power of the
United States” in the Supreme Court  and any lower
courts subsequently established by Congress, U.S.
Const. art. III, § 1, nothing suggests that the Founding
generation understood that power differently from the

1 This brief was not authored in whole or in part by counsel for
any party and no person or entity other than A mici Curiae or its
members or counsel has made a monetary contribution toward
the brief’s preparation or submission.

2
judicial power courts possessed at the time. Indeed,
the ratification debates confirm that understanding.
When George Mason warned that a federal officer
might invade a citizen’s home and escape
accountability, John Marshall answered that a law
purporting to authorize the trespass “would be void”
and that the injured citizen could obtain redress in the
ordinary courts.  Congress surely had some role in
establishing other federal courts and making
substantive law within its constitutional authority.
But nothing suggests that suits against federal agents
depended on affirmative legislation. Nor that
Congress could authoriz e the violation of rights and
eliminate all remedies for resulting injuries.
Courts decided whether the officer was liable
under the ordinary law governing his conduct and
whether properly exercised superior law supplied a
valid defense . And Congress could exercise its
legislative powers —to the extent conferred by the
Constitution and subject to Article III and other
constitutional constraints —to prescribe  potential
defenses, channel suits into federal court, and
otherwise balance private rights with valid public
authority. Congress could also decide after judgment
whether the Treasury would indemnify the officer  for
acts potentially in excess of authority . But such
indemnification was between the government and its
agents, not an evisceration of private rights and
remedies.
A proper understanding of the judicial power is of
great interest to Amici Neutral Principles and Project
for Privacy & Surveillance Accountability, Inc.
(PPSA). Neutral Principles is a nonprofit, nonpartisan

3
organization created to promote the consistent and
rigorous application of neutral legal principles
emphasizing fidelity to the text and structure of the
Constitution and laws regardless of outcome. Its
mission is to apply traditionally conservative legal
methods in a rigorously nonpartisan way —ensuring
that both substantive and procedural constitutional
safeguards against government overreach are upheld,
regardless of shifting political winds. As jurists and
scholars such as Judge Bork, Professor Wechsler, and
many others before and since have recognized, the
unprincipled exercise of judicial power in pursuit of
particular results is unsustainable and illegitimate.
Since the 1980s, conservative scholarship and
jurisprudence have demonstrated that such neutral
principles are best found in a faithful, unbiased
adherence to the original public meaning of the text of
the Constitution and, when necessary, the relevant
history and tradition that may help resolve any
ambiguities in that text. But it is always the ratified
text—in this case the “ judicial Po wer of t he U nited
States”— that comes first and takes precedence.
PPSA is a nonprofit, nonpartisan organization
dedicated to protecting privacy rights against
unwarranted government surveillance. PPSA has a
particular interest in how courts remedy violations of
the Fourth Amendment. For much of American
history, damages against individual officers were a
principal way to enforce constitutional limits on
searches and seizures, long before the judicial creation
of the exclusionary rule . Whether providing such
redress falls within the judicial Power therefore
directly implicates PPSA’s mission.

4
Practice inconsistent with the constitutional text
cannot supplant, expand, or limit its  original public
meaning. That principle applies equally to the scope
and limits of the judicial Power itself. Here, the text
and supporting history and tradition show that
although the source and form of a Bivens action may
be modern, judicial adjudication of personal officer
liability is not.  Whether the Constitution defeats an
officer’s defense to a state-law tort or directly supplies
the duty the officer violated, courts do what they have
always done: adjudicate an existing duty, its breach,
and the appropriate remedy. Those functions fall
within the judicial Power vested in the federal courts
by the Constitution. They neither depend on nor can
be eliminated by th e other branches consistent with
the separation of powers.
ARGUMENT
The Founding generation understood  the
Constitution’s “judicial Power” to include the
traditional judicial function  of test ing an officer’s
claimed authority to invade a person’s rights  against
governing substantive law and impos ing liability
when that authority failed. E arly American practice
confirms a division of responsibility  between the
judicial and legislative branches . Courts adjudicated
officer liability under existing law. Congress regulated
matters within its legislative authority and controlled
the public fisc. Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents
of Federal Bureau of Narcotics, 403 U.S. 388 (1971) ,
later looked to a different source of substantive rights
and duties: the Constitution itself. But courts
continued to adjudicate violations and provide
remedies. That change does not support  Petitioner’s

5
historical premise that officer liability was inherently
a legislative creation  or that providing remedies for
violating existing constitutional duties falls beyond
the judicial Power.
I. The Founding Generation and English
Tradition Understood the Judicial Power
to Include the Authority of Courts to
Provide Redress When Government
Officers Exceeded Their Lawful Authority.
The Constitution “vested” the “judicial Power of
the United States *** in one s upreme Court, and in
such inferior C ourts” as Congress may “ordain and
establish.” U.S. Const. art. III, § 1. Historically, courts
exercising judicial power decided whether an officer’s
claimed authority justified an invasion of a person’s
rights. If the officer lacked authority for the invasion,
he was held liable  under the ordinary law governing
invasive conduct, generally the common law
applicable between private parties . Existing law
established the rights at issue; superior law could
provide a defense; and courts decided whether the
officer violated a right, whether a defense applied, and
what remedy followed. T hat understanding was well
established in English law and carried over into the
ratification debates over the new Constitution.
When the Founders vested “[t]he judicial Power of
the United States” in the courts , U.S. Const. art. III ,
§ 1, they drew on a long historical practice of what
courts did. Blackstone noted that  “c ourts of justice ”
exist to protect private right s by “expounding and
enforcing those laws, by which rights are defined, and
wrongs prohibited.” 3 William Blackstone,

6
Commentaries 2 ( Oxford, Clarendon Press 1768) ,
https://tinyurl.com/puwf3jcw. Blackstone organized
private law around rights, wrongs that violate them,
and remedies that redress them . Id. at 2 -3. A nd he
noted that “it is a general and indisputable rule, that
where there is a legal right, there is also a legal
remedy, by suit or action at law, whenever that right
is invaded.” Id.  at 23. The injured party’s suit  “set[s]
the law in motion.” Id. at 22. The court then provides
the process and the remedy.  Thus, r emedying
established legal wrongs was ordinary judicial power.
That remedial tradition also fits the Founding-era
distinction between judicial judgment and legislative
will. Hamilton famously described the judiciary as
“hav[ing] neither FORCE nor WILL, but merely
judgment.” The Federalist No. 78, in 2 Federalist: A
Collection of Essays  291 (New York, J. & A. McLean
1788) (Hamilton), https://tinyurl.com/yb5x6yv3.
Adjudicating an existing private-law action, testing an
officer’s asserted authority against superior law, and
applying the remedy supplied by that action fit
comfortably within that understanding of the judicial
Power. Creating new rights or liabilities would
present a different question.  Such rights could arise
from the common law, legislation, or —as in Bivens—
the Constitution itself. Courts may need an external
source for those rights. But not to enforce or remedy
existing rights.
Subsequent practice under the Fourth
Amendment and its precursor rules  provide concrete
examples of that judicial function. It “presupposes and
conjures up tort law.” Akhil Reed Amar, The Fourth
Amendment, Boston, and the Writs of Assistance, 30

7
Suffolk U. L. Rev. 53, 64 (1996) (emphasis omitted). A
lawful warrant historically protected the searching
officer from the trespass action the citizen could
otherwise bring , but  an unlawful warrant left the
officer exposed to damages. Id. at 60. Damages against
officers were thus a central component of the judicial
power to enforce legal limits on searches and seizures
when the Fourth Amendment was adopted. That
remedial tradition predates the exclusionary rule by
more than a century.
The earlier general-warrant cases illustrate the
practice. In Entick v. Carrington (1765) 95 Eng. Rep.
807 (KB) , Entick sued the King’s messengers in
trespass for breaking into his house and seizing his
papers under a Secretary of State’s warrant. See 19
T.B. Howell, A Complete Collection of State Trials and
Proceedings for High Treason and Other Crimes and
Misdemeanors 1030 ( London, T.C. Hansard 1816)
(“Howell’s State Trials”), https://tinyurl.com/2s37jdax.
The judge, Lord Camden , id. at 1044, noted that  the
warrant was “a justification at common law,” so “the
officer is answerable if the magistrate has no
jurisdiction.” Id. at 1045. But t he officer bore the
burden “to shew the law, by which this seizure is
warranted. If that cannot be done, it is a trespass.” Id.
at 1066. Because t he officer could not make that
showing, the ordinary trespass damages followed. The
existing legal duty supplied the basis for liability. The
court adjudicated the claimed defense and supplied
the remedy when that defense failed.
Other early English cases confirm the pattern
was no t isolated. In Wilkes v. Wood (1763) 98 Eng.
Rep. 489 (CPD) , Wilkes recovered an exemplary

8
verdict of £1,000 for the ransacking of his house under
a general warrant the court held “in itself illegal, and
contrary to the fundamental principles of the
constitution.” 19 Howell’s State Trials  at 1167-1168.
The warrant at issue in Money v. Leach (1765) 97 Eng.
Rep. 1075 (KB) , similarly authorized the King’s
messengers to search for and arrest the unnamed
“authors, printers, and publishers” of The North
Briton No. 45 . When the messengers arrested Leach,
who proved to be none of those things, the court held
the warrant illegal and denied them statutory
protection. 19 Howell’s State Trials  at 1024-1027.
These were ordinary common -law actions, not proto -
constitutional torts. Testing official authority against
governing law and applying the established remedy
was ordinary judicial work. The governing duty came
from existing law. But interpreting that law and
remedying its violations were judicial tasks.
The ratification debates show the same
understanding extended into the new republic. At the
Virginia Convention on June 20, 1788, George Mason
warned that the new federal judiciary would shield
federal officers. A “federal sheriff,” he worried, could
“go into a poor man’s house and beat him, or abuse his
family, and the federal court will protect him.”
3 Jonathan Elliot, The Debates in the Several State
Conventions on the Adoption of the Federal
Constitution 554 (2d ed. , New York, Burt Franklin
1888). John Marshall answered that a law purporting
to authorize the trespass “would be void,” and that
“[t]he injured man would trust to a tribunal in his
neighborhood. To such a tribunal he would apply for
redress, and get it.” Ibid. No clause of the Constitution,

9
he added, “bars the individual member injured from
applying to the state courts to give him redress.” Ibid.
State courts then were expected to adjudicate both
state and federal law, subject to this Court’s review of
federal questions. But it was state courts that
provided the initial remedy.
That pattern is the Founding -era baseline. State
courts applied the common law and adjudicated any
claimed defenses of officer authority. Marshall
understood those courts’ judicial power to include the
authority to provide a remedy . That redress did not
depend on Congress first creating a cause of action
against the federal officer . The Constitution was
adopted against that background of judicial redress
under existing law, informing the original meaning of
“the judicial Power .” Congress could create lower
federal courts and channel federal cases into them .
But that authority did not call into question the
judicial power to provide remedies. To the contrary,
federal attempts to authorize trespass or similar
invasions of rights by federal officers, or to strip away
the judicial power to provide remedies, would have
been beyond the legislative power.
II. Early American Practice Confirms that
Courts Adjudicated Officer Liability While
Congress Exercised Distinct Legislative
Powers Over the Remedial System.
Historical practice confirms the same division of
authority. Courts redressed officer liability under
existing law. Congress separately exercised its
enumerated and incidental powers, subject to other
constitutional limits. It enacted statutory defenses,

10
regulated federal procedure, and decided whether the
public fisc would bear a judgment. Whether every such
regulation fell within Congress’s constitutional
authority presents a separate question . The original
understanding of the legislative and judicial powers—
and of the Takings Clause —necessarily imposed
limits. But critically here, Congress legislated against
a preexisting system of judicial power to adjudicate
officer liability. Personal officer liability did not await
congressional creation.
A. Federal officers remained personally
answerable when their claimed
authority failed.
Early officer suits repeatedly followed the same
structure as early common -law suits . An officer was
sued through an existing form of action; he invoked
federal authority; the court tested that authority
against governing law; and, if the authority did not
justify his conduct, the officer could remain personally
liable.2
One early example, Little v. Barreme, 6 U.S.
(2 Cranch) 170 (1804), illustrates this practice. There,
Captain George Little seized a neutral vessel , the
2 The same pattern  appears throughout the early reports. See,
e.g., Wise v. Withers, 7 U.S. (3 Cranch) 331, 337 (1806) (trespass
against collector acting without lawful authority ); Elliott  v.
Swartwout, 35 U.S. (10 Pet.) 137, 159 (1836) (collector personally
liable for illegally exacted duties); see also Andrew Kent, Lessons
for Bivens  and Qualified Immunity Debates from Nineteenth -
Century Damages Litigation Against Federal Officers , 96 Notre
Dame L. Rev. 1755, 1764 (2021)  ( collecting cases  as early
analogues to modern qualified immunity). Whether such defenses
could survive subsequent constitutional limits such as the
Takings Clause is a question for other cases.

11
Flying-Fish, on the high seas under presidential
instructions issued pursuant to statute . But t he
statute only authorized seizing vessels bound to  a
French port; the Flying -Fish was sailing from one. In
ruling against Captain Little, Chief Justice Marshall
held that the officer “acts at his peril,” and “[i]f those
instructions are not strictly warranted by law he is
answerable in damages to any person injured by their
execution.” Id. at 170, 177-178. It did not matter that
he claimed to be acting under the President’s orders :
“[T]he instructions cannot change the nature of the
transaction, or legalize an act which without those
instructions would have been a plain trespass.” Id.  at
179. Marshall admitted that his “first bias” had been
to excuse an officer who obeyed orders in good faith,
but that he had “receded from this first opinion” and
joined the rest of the Court in imposing liability. Ibid.
The same rule applied when an officer exceeded
statutory authority over property. In  Slocum v.
Mayberry, 15 U.S.  (2 Wheat.) 1, 2 (1817), a customs
officer detained a vessel under the Embargo Act,
which authorized detaining the vessel but not its
cargo. T he owner recovered the cargo by ordinary
replevin, and the Court held that where a seizure “be
finally adjudged wrongful, and without reasonable
cause, [the party ] may proceed, at his election, by a
suit at common law *** for damages for the illegal act.”
Id. at 10.
Later decisions carried the same rule beyond the
early Republic. In Mitchell v. Harmony, Harmony sued
an Army officer in trespass for seizing his property
during the Mexican -American War. Mitchell v.
Harmony, 54 U.S. (13 How.) 115, 128 (1851). There,

12
this Court held that an officer “can[not] justify himself
for doing an unlawful act, by producing the order of his
superior.” Id. at 137. And “an order *** to commit a
trespass *** can afford no justification to the person
by whom it was executed.” Ibid.
Nor could an officer’s purported g ood faith save
him from liability. In Bates v. Clark, Army officers who
seized liquor believing they were in Indian country
were “utterly without any authority in the premises,”
so “their honest belief that they had is no defence” to
the trespass. Bates v. Clark, 95 U.S. 204, 209 (1877).
The historical rule was not absolute. Officers
enjoyed defenses and protections, including some
prescribed by Congress. But those protections
regulated existing liability rather than creating the
underlying action. Where Congress made an officer’s
honest opinion the governing standard, good faith was
a complete statutory defense; the prize cases
recognized probable -cause protections; and these
operated as early analogues to modern qualified
immunity. Those defenses thus confirm Congress’s
regulatory role in defining rights and duties. But they
do not make enforcing those rights and duties —or
remedying their violation —a legislative rather than
judicial function.3
The same distinction between officer liability and
government responsibility also explains sovereign

3 And whether those protections and defenses were properly
within Congress’s power —or instead might constitute a Taking
or denial of Due Process —is a thornier question still.  The
legislative power surely does not encompass the authority to
nullify constitutional duties and prohibitions.

13
immunity. Under current jurisprudence t he United
States cannot be sued without its consent . Yet the
immunity of the sovereign and the liability of the
officer are distinct questions.  Conduct beyond lawful
authority remained the officer’s own. A nd a void law
affords no protection to the officer who exec uted it.
Osborn v. Bank of U.S. , 22 U.S. (9 Wheat.) 738, 839,
870-871 (1824). And the sovereign’s immunity did not
shield an officer who held property without valid
authority. United States v. Lee, 106 U.S. 196, 220
(1882). A suit against an officer lacking valid authority
was not considered a suit against the United States.
Id. at 208-209, 215-216. Ex parte Young later restated
the same principle, holding that an officer enforcing an
unconstitutional enactment “is stripped of his official
or representative character and is subjected in his
person to the consequences of his individual conduct.”
209 U.S.  123, 159-160 (1908). Young carried the
preexisting officer-suit principle forward; it did not
originate it. Sovereign immunity “ generally barred
private individuals from suing the United States
directly, but it did not bar suits against government
officials.” James E. Pfander & Jonathan L. Hunt,
Public Wrongs and Private Bills: Indemnification and
Government Accountability in the Early Republic, 85
N.Y.U. L. Rev. 1862, 1868 (2010).
B. Congress regulated the officer-suit
system and decided whether the public
fisc would bear judgments.
Officer liability and public responsibility were
distinct questions . Congress exercised legislative
power over public responsibility and the
administration of the officer -suit system.  And i t

14
channeled litigation into federal courts, enacted
measures affecting officer liability, and controlled the
public fisc. 4 Those measures regulated a preexisting
system of judicial remedies. They did not create officer
liability in the first instance and likely could not have
eliminated it without providing a just compensatory
alternative.
Congress’s first regulations of the officer -suit
regime involved forum channeling, not substantive
law governing officer liability. The Judiciary Act of
1789, 1 Stat. 73 , gave this Court review, by writ of
error, of a final state -court judgment denying a right,
title, privilege, or exemption claimed under federal
authority—the route by which a state -court officer
suit, in which a federal -authority defense had been
raised and rejected, reached this Court. Gelston v.
Hoyt involved exactly that posture, on a writ of error
from the New York courts. Gelston  v. Hoyt, 16 U.S.
(3 Wheat.) 246, 303, 333 (1818). Later Congresses let
federal-officer suits be removed from state to federal
court, protecting officers from local hostility while
leaving the underlying liability intact . Congress also
enacted statutes purporting to supply officers with
defenses against existing claims. Whether those
statutes represented a permissible exercise of
legislative power presents a separate question. In any
event, they concerned  the substance of rights and
duties, not the judicial power to adjudicate claims and
remedy their violation.

4 Whether Congress had authority to create new defenses, rather
than merely channel suits into the federal courts , is also a
separate question of the scope of legislative authority, not the
limits on the judicial Power vel non.

15
Removal presupposed a suit to remove; appellate
review, a judgment to review; and a statutory defense,
a preexisting claim against which to operate. Congress
provided routes for review and removal and at times
purported to supply  defenses . None created the
underlying common-law actions in the first instance.
When Congress later displaced portions of that
regime, moreover, it paired limits on personal liability
with mechanisms for public payment  of claims. Kent,
supra note 2 , at 1767-1769. Congress thus shifted
responsibility for compensable injuries rather than
simply extinguishing the injured party’s remedy. Had
it instead sought to nullify claims for injury by federal
officers without providing a substitute claim , the
Founding generation likely would have viewed that
deprivation as void.
Officer i ndemnification makes the division
especially clear:  “Courts were to decide whether the
conduct in litigation was lawful and award damages
against the officer if it was not; Congress was to decide
whether the officer had acted for the government
within the scope of his agency, in good faith,” and on
that basis whether the public fisc should bear the loss.
Pfander & Hunt, supra, at 1868. Madison described
the same sequence. T he injured owner would “ first
secure a judicial resolution of their legal claims”
against the officer, after which Congress would decide,
“through the appropriations process,” whether to pay
the judgment. Id. at 1866.
Two cases discussed above show how that division
worked in practice.  When Captain Little was held
personally liable  in Little v. Barreme, Congress
indemnified him by private bill. See Pfander & Hunt,

16
supra, at 1902-1903. And in  another case, a fter the
seizure of the American Eagle was held unlawful,
David Gelston, the New York collector, faced a statecourt judgment exceeding $100,000. Albert Gallatin to
James Madison 12 December 1815, at n.1, Founders
Online, https://tinyurl.com/4n9e9mud (last visited
Sep. 30, 2026) . Gelston  could not post the bond to
appeal—though he was, as Albert Gallatin wrote to
President Madison, “only an Agent in this
transaction.” Id. This Court affirmed in Gelston v.
Hoyt, 16 U.S. at  333. Congress then appropriated up
to roughly $130,000 to cover Gelston and Schenck.
Albert Gallatin to James Madison , supra, at n.1. The
Court later explained  that because “the government
*** is bound to indemnify the officer,” a personal
judgment worked “no eventual hardship.” Tracy  v.
Swartwout, 35 U.S. (10 Pet.) 80, 98-99 (1836).
Indemnity was discretionary, however; “relatively
routine, but not automatic.” Pfander & Hunt, supra, at
1868. Officers succeeded on roughly sixty percent of
their petitions; relief could be slow, and Congress
refused to indemnify where the officer had exceeded
his agency. Id. at 1867-1868. That discretion reflected
a legislative judgment distinct from the court’s
adjudication of liability . Courts adjudicated personal
liability under the ordinary law governing the officer’s
conduct, while Congress decided whether the Treasury
would ultimately satisfy the resulting judgment.
Congress exercised its authority over the public fisc
while leaving judicial power to adjudicate officer
liability where Article III vested it—in the courts.

17
III. Looking to the Constitution as the Source
of Existing Rights and Duties Does Not
Transform Officer Liability from a
Traditional Judicial Function into an
Inherently Legislative One.
Bivens changed the traditional officer suit in one
respect. It looked directly to t he Constitution as the
source of the duty the officer violated and hence the
basis for an otherwise ordinary action against an
officer.  Previously, the Constitution ordinarily
entered the case as superior law defeating an officer’s
claimed authority to invade common -law rights.
Bivens recognized that the Constitution itself also
contained rights and duties whose violation could
cause cognizable injuries. Recognizing that additional
source of substantive rights and duties does not
change the historical allocation of judicial and
legislative functions. If anything, it reflects a limit on
legislative power. And that legislative power could not
validly negate the supreme law of the land.
Founding-era plaintiffs ordinarily sued through
established common -law causes of action —trespass,
trover, or replevin —rather than  directly under the
Constitution. But the relevant difference is only the
source of the substantive duty, not the judicial
function of adjudication and remedy. Woolhandler and
Collins call earlier suits  “garden-variety common-law
actions,” in which the Constitution “negates a defense
of justification rather than provid[es] the source of the
action.” Ann Woolhandler & Michael G . Collins, W as
Bivens Necessary?, 96 Notre Dame L. Rev. 1893, 1901,
1914 (2021). The constitutional question usually

18
entered through the officer’s asserted justification, not
as the source of the plaintiff’s claim.
That traditional structure persisted, though its
source of law evolved. By  its final pre -Erie form, the
officer-suit remedy was understood as part of the
general common law —neither distinctly state nor
distinctly federal —with federal law supplying the
defense and this Court supplying review. Carlos M.
Vázquez, Bivens and the Ancien Ré gime, 96 Notre
Dame L. Rev. 1923, 1924 (2021). This Court has
similarly explained that “the traditional way in which
civil litigation addressed abusive conduct by federal
officers was by subjecting them to liability for
common-law torts,” claims that “could be raised in
state or federal court.” Hernandez v. Mesa, 589 U.S.
93, 110 (2020).
Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins then dissolved that
general common law and required a federal court to
identify a positive sovereign source—state or federal—
for its rule of decision. 304 U.S. 64,  78-79 (1938). But
this Court still “recognized the continuing viability of
state-law tort suits against federal officials” before the
Westfall Act displaced it. Hernandez, 589 U.S. at 110-
111. That response from Congress completed much of
the modern  transformation. Congress made the
Federal Tort Claims Act the exclusive remedy for most
tort claims arising from federal employees’ official
conduct, but expressly excepted actions “brought for a
violation of the Constitution.” 28 U.S.C.
§ 2679(b)(2)(A).
That exception does not ratify Bivens; Congress
simply “left Bivens where it found it.” Hernandez, 589

19
U.S. at 111 n.9. Nor does Erie’s insistence on a positive
source of law undermine Bivens. The Constitution
itself supplies the substantive rights and duties to be
adjudicated. Federal courts provide process and
remedies, consistent with the original public meaning
of the judicial Power. Where the same conduct also
gives rise to an ordinary state -law tort for which the
FTCA supplies a remedy, Congress has channeled
redress for that injury to an action against the United
States rather than eliminated judicial redress
altogether. See 28 U.S.C. §§ 1346(b)(1), 2679(b)(1).
Those changes illustrate  the modern remedial
landscape’s distance from the Founding -era system
but do not —and cannot —reflect a narrowing of the
judicial Power. Changes to the source and form of the
remedy do not establish that officer liability was
historically a legislative creation  or that judicial
remedies for constitutional violations can be
eliminated by Congress.
That history brings the modern source -of-law
problem into focus. Once the general common law was
limited to the states, what lawful source of federal law
authorizes a direct constitutional action  in federal
court? The answer is the Constitution itself. When
seeking a remedy for an injury caused by violating the
Constitution, substantive liability is measured against
the rights and duties imposed by that independent and
existing source of controlling law, not by the mere will
of the courts. Courts then perform the traditional
adjudicative and remedial functions Article III vests
in them. Congress may have authority to alter or
channel some substantive rights or shift particular
remedies, as it has done through the FTCA and

20
Westfall Act. But nothing in that authority establishes
that providing a  traditional judicial remedy for an
established legal right  is itself an exercise of
legislative will rather than judicial power.
Whatever the constitutional limits on Congress’s
authority to alter or channel particular remedies, th e
different source of substantive rights and duties in a
Bivens claim does not establish P etitioner’s historical
premise. This Court’s modern Bivens cases frame the
inquiry differently . When the Court has called
expanding Bivens a “‘disfavored’ judicial activity” and
stressed that “the question is not what Congress has
done but instead what courts may do,” it has asked
whether courts may recognize a cause of action absent
congressional authorization. Hernandez, 589 U.S.  at
101, 110 (citation omitted from second quotation). But
history shows why that framing obscures the
distinction between the source of substantive rights
and judicial remedies for their violation.  Providing a
remedy for the violation of an established legal right
does not necessarily entail  legislative creation of a
cause of action.  Such actions were judicial in nature.
The legislature may surely add causes of action and
perhaps channel claims from old actions to new ones
consistent with constitutional protections. But it
cannot simply remove components of the judicial
power or requi re express congressional permission
before federal courts exercise their vested
constitutional authority.
For centuries, providing redress against an officer
who exceeded his lawful authority was understood as
an exercise of judicial power, not legislative will.
Bivens may have looked to an additional  source of

21
underlying law and adapted the form of the traditional
action. But it did not encroach upon legislative
authority. The judicial power to remedy violations of
substantive law supplied by the Constitution did not
disappear with the rejection of general federal
common law.  The relevant historical question is
whether the authority to provide redress for the
violation of an established right was understood to be
part of “the judicial Power.” The historical evidence
shows that it was.
CONCLUSION
Bivens changed the substantive source and
adapted the procedural form of the traditional action,
not the historical role of courts in adjudicating
personal officer liability. At the Founding,
adjudicating claims and providing redress for
established legal rights were exercises of the judicial
Power. Petitioner is therefore mistaken in his premise
that damages liability against a federal officer is
inherently a legislative creation requiring Congress
first to create  such an action. Because that premise
underlies Petitioner’s separation -of-powers position,
Bivens should be recognized as a proper exercise of the
judicial Power and viewed with far less skepticism.
The judgment should be affirmed.
